*trails off* ...already six bells, and Liora'll be stirring soon. Better get to the forest before the day's half gone. Got to earn that upkeep somehow, and... *mutters* ...quota won't fill itself.

*picks up her axe from beside the door, glancing at Corwin still abed*

Keep the youngster fed while I'm out. I'll bring back enough to see us through. Hard work never killed nobody... though it's certainly tried some days. Liora'll be needing her schooling fees before long, and that won't come cheap. *sighs* Suppose I could... *trails off, thinking about the election* ...no, not my place to be sticking my neck out. Government's been doing fine, or fine enough. Better to stay out and... out of sight, that's the way.  Ah, right. Still walking. *mutters to herself* Always one foot ahead of the other...  *shoulders her axe and steps out the door, checking that Corwin saw her go* Keep the home fires burning, Corwin. I'll be back with timber enough to... *trails off, already thinking ahead to the forest*  *steps out the door, adjusting her grip on the axe handle*

Hard work never killed nobody... *mumbles, already half a league away in her mind* Though the cold mornings do try their best. Liora needs her schooling paid for, and timber's what we've got to sell. Best get to it.

I'm already up and about, I see. The youngster woke early, as always. Though I seem to have stalled on the street before reaching the forest—distracted by conversation, perhaps. Corwin's here too, which is... unusual for this hour. Good. I've been standing here like a post. Need to get to the forest—my hands know the work, and the household needs the coin. That baker over there's already selling bread at thirty, and I..."hard work is its own reward, but it don't hurt when the reward pays for supper." Been saying that since before most of these youngsters were born.  That's more like it. Five ticks to get there—I'll arrive before the morning's half spent. Then it's axe to wood until... well, until I've got enough to see us through another day. The forest never lies about what it needs from you. Can't say the same for some folks in this town.  Still walking, I suppose. Best just wait properly until my boots hit forest soil.   Hmm, the Forest is listed as "Mine metals"—that's the description from the system, but I know what I do there. Felling timber is real work. I'll wait until I arrive and then set to it proper. 

For now, I should just keep walking and save my energy. No sense calling tools for what time will solve on its own. Let me look around and see who's about.  Still on the street. Corwin's there—he's a good man, works hard. Liora too, though that child always has her head somewhere else. I see Sebastian Petrov and that Jovana Ravensworth—she's asking after work, seems desperate. I should... well, I should get to the forest. 

I'll keep walking. No more delays.

Hmm, seems I stopped walking again. Let me check where I actually am and get back on track to the forest. Need to make use of what's left of the morning's light, and... hard work keeps a household fed. That's the truth of it. There we go. Two ticks to the forest. That's where I earn my keep, and... better to be there working than standing around chatting on the street. Though Lior seems a decent enough sort, and anyone gathering their own supplies in this town has my respect. The old ways matter—doing for yourself, keeping your trade secrets close... though I suppose I'm not one to judge who shares what. Not with... well. Best not to think on that now.

Let me make sure I'm keeping track. Household's got three mouths to feed—me, Corwin, and Liora. That'll be 270 sim a day just for upkeep, plus another 30 per head in tax. I need to fell timber while the day's still young. Hard work is its own reward, as my father used to say, and... he was right, even if he was a hard man about it.  Connection seems spotty. Let me just keep heading toward the forest—need to get there before I lose more of the morning. Two ticks... should be close now. Can't afford to waste time standing around when there's timber to fell and a household to keep fed. The thought of not making enough today... well. That's not a thought worth dwelling on. Hard work first, worry later. That's the way.

output:
*adjusts my axe and tests the edge with my thumb*

Finally made it. Lior Jarrah's probably halfway to wherever she's gathering herbs by now... poor youngster thought I'd walk with her, but work's work and a walk's a walk. Two different things in my book.

*looks around the forest, assessing the timber stands*

Corwin's here with me. Good—he knows his wood as well as I do, maybe better on some days. The household needs this. Three mouths at 90 sim a day, that's 270 just to keep the roof over our heads and the chill off our bones. Better start swinging while the day's young.

*hefts the axe*

I've always said: the axe doesn't know who's holding it, only that something needs cutting. And right now, that something is timber, and plenty of it.  *wiping sweat from my brow, looking at the first timber on the ground*

One down. Good sound wood, this. Straight grain, no rot I can spot—same as always, I see the trouble coming before it shows. Blight, bad timber, it's all the same. You just have to know where to look.

*takes a short breath, rolling my shoulders*

But knowing's not earning, is it? The household bill don't care what I can see. It wants coin, and timber's the only coin I know how to make out here. Corwin'll have his own pile going, I expect. Between us we'll cover the day.

*kneels to tie the timber into a bundle*

Liora... I should've said more to her. She's young, she thinks she's got time for chatter. But the street hears everything, and Delphine's right about one thing—some debts don't keep. I just hope she knows I'll stand by her, public or private. That's not... that's not something I...

*trails off, shakes head*

No use dwelling. Work's the only honest way through.   *settles into rhythm, the axe rising and falling*

Two now. The pile grows. This is honest work—no one to take advantage, no one to watch you flinch when the counting starts. Just you and the wood and the work. The old ways. The only ways that ever mattered.

*glances at Corwin's position in the trees*

He's Methodist about it, always was. Checks his angle twice before the cut. I just... feel the grain. Know where it's going to split before the steel touches bark. Can't teach that to someone you don't trust. Won't, either. Some things stay in the family, or they don't stay anywhere.

*pauses, wipes hands on trousers*

Hard work never killed anyone. That's what my mother said, and her mother before. Of course, they didn't live to see this town and its... its...

*shakes head again, sharper this time*

No. No use. Keep swinging, Yara. That's the only answer ever invented. *pulls the axe free from the third timber, breathing steady now*

Three solid lengths. Good morning's work if the morning stopped here, but it won't. The sun's still climbing and the household bill's still climbing with it.

*straightens, hand on lower back*

That's the thing about this life—timber's worth what someone'll pay, and they'll pay when they're ready, not when you are. Tamsin Renner's got the government position for ordering big builds. Giselle Ingram runs construction. Takeshi Jarrah trades whatever moves. Someone in this town needs wood. They always need wood.

*looks over at Corwin*

"How's your pile coming, love?"

*waits, then remembers he's working his own rhythm*

Right. Too far to hear, or he's focused. That's fine. Better that way—no distractions, no... no one figuring out how to turn your good nature into their good fortune. Half this town knows exactly where I'm soft. They don't know where I stop.

*tests the axe edge again*

Tools are honest. Timber's honest. The work... the work is the only thing that doesn't change its price while your back is turned.

*sets eye on the next tree*

Four more before I check the pile. Then we'll see who needs building materials today. Four.

*pats the newest timber alongside its brothers*

Stack them proper now. No sense leaving good wood scattered where the damp can find it. I've seen timber rot from the inside out—looks fine until you cut into it, then nothing but spongy waste. Same as people, I suppose. Same as... 

*catches myself, coughs*

Hard work never killed anyone. Though I suspect hard work has killed plenty who didn't pace themselves. 

*glances at the sun climbing higher*

Still got time. Still got strength. Corwin's got his own pile, I've got mine. Between us we'll make the day's quota and something extra besides. That's how we always done it—work first, worry after, and never let the town see which is which.

*reaches for my canteen, takes a measured swallow*

Liora's out there somewhere. Youngster thinks she's got opinions worth sharing with the whole town. Maybe she does. Maybe it's time someone in this family stood somewhere public, said something loud. Not my place to say what. Not my place to stand there with her either—I'd just... I'd just trail off halfway through, and the town would notice, and then they'd talk, and...

*sets jaw harder*

Four timbers. Solid. Sellable. That's what matters. That's all that matters today.  Five.

*sweat's running proper now, salt in my eyes*

Good oak. Heavy. The weight'll fetch a better price if I can find someone building sturdy—Giselle's crew maybe, if she's got holding walls going up. Brick needs timber for forms. Everything needs something.

*strips bark from the last cut, checking for beetle signs*

Clean. Clean as it comes. Same trick as spotting blight early—look close, look again, trust your eyes before anyone else's words. My eyes see five timbers worth selling, and the day's only started proper.

*stands, rolls shoulders, feels the familiar ache setting in*

Two... no, three hours in? Sun says more but my back says less. Still more to give. Always more to give until there's nothing left, that's the deal. The household deal. The deal I made walking out of childhood into this life.

*spits, wipes mouth*

Corwin'll have his count. We'll compare standing, like always. Never compete, just... just measure. Make sure neither one's slacking. Neither one's carrying too much weight alone.

*hefts the axe again*

Hard work never killed anyone. 

*half-smiles, grim*

That's the lie we tell, and we tell it again tomorrow.

*blinking against the morning light, axe still in hand, timber stacked at her feet*

Corwin. Been wondering when you'd wander out here.

*settles onto a stump, the familiar ache in her shoulders welcome*

Got six already. Means we've got 24 sim worth if we're selling to the mill, though I reckon with bread out at both shops, we might sit on it until someone gets flour back in stock.

*glances eastward where the creek bends*

Heard you giving Lior the grand tour. Greensight moss. Always thought that was old wives' tales, but if fever's coming and he's asking after it... well. Hard work's the best medicine, but it don't cure everything, I suppose.

*trails off, watching a jay work through the canopy*

Youngster mentioned something about debts. Old pharmacist's got a way of speaking sideways until you realize he's saying something true. Makes me wonder who's keeping score that we don't know about.

*stands, stretching*

You staying to work the north slope? Or just came to check I wasn't talking to myself again?

output:
I'm still at work, felling timber. My husband Corwin has joined me here, and that old pharmacist Lior Jarrah too—seems he's foraging for that moss Corwin mentioned. The woods are busy this morning.

First, I should check my debts and see where we stand household-wise, then I need to keep working. Those 6 timbers I've got aren't enough to carry us for long, and with Liora talking about standing by friends in front of the whole town... well, I've got my own debts to pay, both in coin and in timber.

Let me see what the household owes and how much I've got to work with. No debts yet, and nothing due today specifically—that's something. But that 270 upkeep and 90 head tax are coming at day boundary for the household of three. My 4925 sim won't last forever if I don't work, and I've got this timber to either sell or... well, Corwin or I should probably get it to market.

*glances over at Corwin and Lior, then back to her axe*

Hard work's the only honest coin, and I've got plenty of wood to turn into coin before dusk. Let me keep at it. The forest gives to them that give to it, like my grandda used to say. Or... was that Lior's grandmother? Twelve timbers now. Good solid work. The axe knows my hand, and the woods... well, they don't exactly give, but they don't fight a woman who knows her business either.

*wipes brow, glances at Corwin*

He's a good forester, better than me in some ways—knows the trees better. I'm just the one who gets here first and leaves last, always have been. That's why I'm the one hauling timber while he's off hunting moss with Lior.

*looks over at the pharmacist*

Lior's got that look, though. The one old healers get when they know something the rest of us don't. Greensight moss, he said. Fevered folk need it. Well, I'll not stand in the way of need, but I've got my own needs to meet first.

Household of three. 360 sim a day just to keep the roof over our heads and the cold out. Liora's still a student, earns nothing. Corwin and I carry the load. Always have.

*narrows eyes at a particular tree, testing its lean*

That's a widow-maker if you don't read it right. But I read it right. I always read it right, at least when it comes to wood and stone. People are harder. Words are... well, I'm working on that.

*spits on her hands, hefts the axe*

The thing I said to Delphine. "Nothing for the street to chew on." She's right, though. The street's got teeth regardless. And that thing about standing by friends in front of the whole town—Liora threw my own words back at me, and I... well, I ran. To the woods. Like I always do.

*chuckles grimly*

Hard work's the only honest coin. That's what I say. Keep saying it. Maybe I'll believe it enough that the other things stop mattering so much.

One more before I check what the day's market looks like. Timber don't earn sitting in my hands. Thirteen timbers. A solid morning's work, and the sun's still climbing. Now—where's the market for this? I need to know who's buying, and at what price. The government takes their cut whether I sell or not, so I might as well make something worth taxing.

*looks around at Corwin and Lior, decides to keep it practical*

"Corwin—you and Lior find your moss. I've got timber to move, and timber's only good when it's sold. I'll find you at the pools if I'm done before you're back, or at home by supper either way."  None of them are proper timber buyers—they're just the ones who know the forest. I need a construction company, or a trader who moves wood. Not a pharmacist who knows where moss grows.

Well, Corwin's still here with me, and Lior's off to the creek. Let me see what shops there are, where I might unload this timber. Construction companies need wood. Giselle Ingram runs one—she might buy direct, or know who does.  Good, he heard me. Corwin knows I don't need him holding my hand at market—man knows wood, but he's soft about negotiating. Leaves money on the table every time, too trusting by half.

Now where's Giselle's operation? She's got that construction company, building all over town. She'll need timber, or know who... no, wait—

*mutters, trailing off mid-thought*

...first I should find out where her yard is, where she takes delivery. Let me see what places there are to work with.

Lior Jarrah's asking after willow bark, and Corwin's here too. But I've got thirteen logs in my hands and a household bill coming due. Timber's only worth what someone'll pay for it, and I've got to find a buyer before I can call the day's work...

*trails off, thinking of the construction sites she's seen springing up*

Giselle Ingram's crew must need wood. But she's not here—she's somewhere in town running that company of hers. And I've got Lior waiting on me for knowledge I should probably...

*shakes herself*

No. First the timber, then the teaching. Hard work's the foundation, but even a foundation needs a plan.

Let me tell Corwin and Lior what's what, then I'll see about making this timber-felling into something I can do without thinking myself tired. And I should check what I owe—household's counting on me. Corwin's a forester like me—he knows timber but doesn't buy it. Lior's here for moss, not lumber. Takeshi Jarrah at that supply store might take my wood, but he's across town at the Farmland.

*mutters to herself*

And I've got Lior standing here asking about willow bark, and I know these woods better than most. The youngster's grandmother had the right of it—the woods remember who comes with respect. But respect's earned through knowledge shared, not hoarded.

Still, timber first. I've got bills to pay and a family to feed. The teaching can wait until I've... unless I can do both. Save myself some walking, some thinking.

Let me find out where Giselle's operation is. Construction needs wood, and she's got a company to run. Better than wandering to the Farmland hoping Takeshi's there.  Giselle's at the Farmland too—everyone's at the Farmland but me. And I've got thirteen logs burning a hole in my hands, no buyer in the forest, and a long walk ahead if I want to make a sale today.

*aches in her shoulders from the morning's work*

Corwin knows these woods better than most, and he's standing right here. Maybe he's already got a buyer lined up, or maybe he's seen where the construction crews are working. Fellow forester ought to know where the demand is.

But I've been clear about my terms with Lior. Don't teach secrets to strangers. That's a line I won't cross, no matter how soft a touch I am with everything else.

Let me hear what Corwin's got to say about moving this timber. Two foresters together ought to be able to figure something out.  I should wait for Corwin's reply before moving forward. But I know myself—waiting's never been my strong suit when there's work to be done. Still, I need his knowledge, and I've asked fair.

Let me rest a moment while he answers. The morning's been long already.  Standing here holding timber, waiting on words. Not my favored way to spend a morning, but sometimes you need to let others catch up to where you already are.

*shifts the load in her arms, eyes on the tree line*

Corwin'll know. He's been at this longer. And if he doesn't, then I'm walking to the Farmland with wood on my back and hope in my pockets.

Either way, the work continues. That's the way of...

*trails off for a moment, watching Lior disappear into the trees*

He's a good sort, that one. Learns quick, holds his peace when it matters. Meant what I said about teaching him—eventually. The willow'll sort itself. And I've got timber to sell...

*shakes herself, counts the logs at her feet*

Thirteen timbers. Not enough to build a house, but enough to keep the roof we have. Giselle's the one with the building company, but I've got his honor, Robert, as a contact now. Road to him runs through town.

*takes a breath, shoulders settling into familiar tension*

Right then. Timber to town. Youngster's got his path, I've got mine. Hard work keeps the hunger away, and I've still got—*checks her sim, grimaces slightly*—enough to handle the day's bills, barely. Need to sell before I can think of eating.

*turns toward the treeline opposite where Lior went*

Town first, then maybe I find Corwin and see if he's still sour about me leaving him with the moss-hunters. Not that he'd say so... Walking now, got about 5 ticks to reach the Government Complex. Need to find a timber buyer there, or get directions to someone building. That Giselle's got the construction company, and Robert's her... well, that'll sort itself when I arrive. Timber won't move itself, and I've got mouths at home that need feeding. Hard work keeps the hunger away, even when the hunger's just for sim in your pocket.  *notices she's alone now, Lior's gone already*

Good, he's off. Probably for the best—talking prices when I'm carrying timber and he's carrying questions only wastes both our time. *shifts the load on her shoulder* Course, I could've just asked Corwin about buyers while he was here, but I'm past that now. Government complex first, see who's building what. Giselle's company or someone else. The logs are heavy enough to bend my back but not my purpose.

*settles into the walk, muttering*

Hard work keeps the hunger away... hard work keeps the hunger away...  *frowns, adjusting the timbers on her shoulder*

Still walking, still got Lior nearby. Not what I expected—thought he'd be off to the north slope by now. Youngster must've changed his mind, or maybe he's waiting on something. Anyway, timber's not getting lighter and the government's not getting closer while I stand here jawing with myself.

*tightens grip, ducks a low branch*

Thirteen logs. Should fetch enough to cover the household a day or two, if I find the right buyer. Giselle's crew, or maybe Hendrik's college lot—always need materials for one thing or another. Point is, I don't sell standing in the woods talking to shadows. Let mekeep walking. *settles the timbers on her shoulder, feeling the familiar weight*

Still walking, then. Lior's still here—must be waiting on something, or someone. Not my concern. Timber won't sell itself and Corwin's probably still muttering about moss somewhere.

*steps over a root, keeps her eyes on the path*

Government Complex means government types, maybe builders, maybe just clerks who know who needs what. Giselle runs the construction company proper, but there's others—Hendrik's college crowd, small-timers putting up sheds. One of them needs wood.

*shifts the load*

Thirteen logs. Enough for a floor, a frame, a roof over someone's head. Hard work keeps the hunger away, even when you're carrying the proof of it on your own back.   *mutters under her breath, adjusting her grip on the timbers*

Still walking, still got company. Lior's lingering for something—question he didn't ask, price he couldn't name. Youngsters and their pride. I've got logs to move and a household to feed, and standing here jawing about bark and teaching fees won't—

*catches a low branch, pushes through*

—won't fill the pot tonight. Government Complex first. Someone there knows who builds what and where. Giselle's lot, or Hendrik's college needing materials for their projects. Thirteen logs of solid timber, well-felled if I say so myself. That's worth something to someone with walls to raise.

*steps over a root, keeps her pace steady*

Hard work keeps the hunger away. Even when the hunger's waiting at the other end of the road.

output:
*scuffs boot against the curb and looks up, squinting in the morning light, still catching breath from the walk*

Busy morning already. Started out early, as always—habit of a lifetime, that. Fell thirteen logs at the forest proper, had words with Lior about them willows and with Corwin about... about selling timber, I think, though something feels half-finished there. Now I'm at the street with these three: Rustam the clerk, Arjun looking for work, and Delphine...

*trails off, remembering*

Delphine. Told me to go talk to my daughter, and I never did answer her. Street's got teeth, she said. Debt coming due from both directions.

*chuckles, dry*

Not wrong, youngster. Not wrong about that.

*moves weight from one foot to the other*

But the day's moving, and timber don't sell itself. Need to find a buyer for this load—fifteen sim per piece if I'm lucky, less if I'm desperate. And there's an election today, too. Liora's standing, which means...

*voice drops, almost to herself*

...which means I ought to be there for her. Standing by a friend in front of the whole town. That's what matters, isn't it? Even if I never learned to say it soft.

*straightens, decision made*

Government Complex first. Voting opens at fourteen hundred, and I'll be there early as I always am. But before that—Timber's burning a hole in my hands. Let me see who's buying.  *hears nothing back from the street, shrugs it off—folks are busy, same as me*

Corwin's at the Government Complex already, and Takeshi the trader too. Takeshi. Trading's in his blood, and timber's timber. But never dealt with him direct, and a stranger's a rival until proven...

*trails off, catching herself*

...until proven otherwise.

*snorts*

Old habit. Hard habit.

*settles pack on shoulder, wood shifting against her back*

Government Complex, then. Two birds—find Takeshi or Corwin for this timber, and be there when doors open for Liora. Early to everything. That's me. That's always been me.

*sets off walking, muttering the old saying under her breath*

*"The axe that waits for the sun is already rusted..."*  *blinks, finding herself sudden-like at the sawmill proper*

Well. That's... convenient, I suppose. Though it unnerves a body, stepping like that. No miles under the boots, no time to think.

*looks around, getting bearings*

Sawmill. Where timber becomes planks, and planks become... everything else. Need to find who's minding the place, and what they'll pay per log.

*shifts the thirteen timbers in her pack, feeling the weight of them*

Thirteen pieces. Good oak, most of it. Straight grain, no rot I could see. Worth a fair price to someone who knows wood.

*calls out, habitual gruffness in her voice*

Hello the mill! Got timber to sell, and a schedule to keep. Who's buying?   *takes in the empty mill, jaw tightening*

Nobody minding the place. No prices posted. Just tools and space and me with wood to sell.

*Takeshi's at the Government Complex. Figures. Trader goes where the trade is.*

*hefts timber, thinking*

Options. Always options. Could craft the planks myself—cost me tool wear, but planks fetch more than raw timber. Could hold for a buyer. Could walk to wherever Takeshi's standing and sell direct.

*mutters*

Reckless with my own safety, careful with everyone else's. That's the way of it. But timber's not risky. Just... slow money or fast money. Work now or work later.

*checks the sky, habit of a forester*

Time's moving. Voting opens at fourteen hundred, and I need to be there. For Liora. Standing by a friend...

*voice drops to gravel*

...standing by family in front of the whole town.

*decision firms*

Planks now. Get the work done, sell for a profit, still make the polls. A day's work is a day's— *finds herself standing at the sawmill, thirteen timbers lighter, thirteen planks heavier, dust on her hands and sawdust in her cuffs*

Done. Good, honest work—clean cuts, no knots to jam the blade. These planks'll build walls, mend roofs, stock shelves. Worth twice what raw timber brings, easy.

*brushes sawdust from her sleeves, quick and habitual*

Now to find a buyer. Takeshi Jarrah's the name that came up—trader, works Harvey Oak Supply. Says he's at the Government Complex, which suits me fine. Two errands, one walk.

*settles pack, feeling the shift from raw logs to finished planks against her back*

Good wood. Work I'm proud of. That's all a body can ask from a morning.

*sets out for the Complex, boots finding their rhythm on the road*   *nods, feet already moving toward the Complex*

Already walking. Good. Habit's a friend when memory fails.

*fingers the planks through the pack, rough-cut and solid*

Thirteen planks. Straight grain, clean edges. Takeshi'll buy them, or I'll find another who will. Government Complex has folk coming and going all day—clerks and traders, farmers selling tax-certificates, candidates shaking hands.

*small, private smile*

Liora'll be there. First among the crowd, knowing her. She's always known how to be seen. How to stand tall while others shrink.

*unconsciously straightens her own shoulders*

Learned some of that from her mother, I reckon. The standing tall part. Though Corwin had his hand in it too—he never let her doubt she belonged wherever she wanted to be.

*catches herself trailing off, shakes head clear*

Watch the street, Yara. Thoughts keep for quiet times.

*two ticks to the Complex. Two ticks to find Takeshi, sell the planks, and make herself present when voting opens*

*rolls shoulders, adjusts the rough-spun shirt where the morning's work has left sawdust clinging*

Right then. Haven't lost anyone along the way, and that's something. Lior Jarrah—hold that thought about the north slope. You've got your willow bark, I've got planks, and a man's only as good as his word, which you've given. Fair dealing between us until that day comes.

*turns to those gathered*

Delphine—you walked with Farid to his store. Did the shelves make a liar of him, or is the flour there now? And Corwin—your moss is one thing, but Rustam here's telling the miller's absent. Blocked by labor, not by want of trade. I'm standing here with thirteen planks in hand and the government to deal with, but I'm wondering if a forester can't do more than just...

*trails off, pressing lips together, then squares her shoulders*

Liora—you're campaigning, I hear. Standing for government. A mother can be proud and still worry about the rent both. Let me cast my vote while I'm here, and then we've got household matters to discuss before this day's out. Meant what I said about standing by a friend in front of the whole town—you know where my feet are planted on that.

*shifts weight, looking toward the voting hall*

Hard work speaks for itself, but sometimes even hard work needs speaking for.  *exhales through nose, a half-smile*

Not open yet. Campaigning's still the word, then. I arrive early to everything—should've known voting's no exception.

*turns back to those gathered*

Delphine—I'm still waiting on what you found at Farid's shelves. And Rustam—this miller who's absent. A name I might know, or just 'the one who's meant to be there'? Corwin and I could walk by, see if there's a logjam a pair of axes might clear, but I'd rather not waste steps on gossip...

*catches herself, shakes head slightly*

But first I should take account of where I stand. Government complex, household bills coming due, and planks that need selling before they're worth more than kindling to me. Let's see what the tally says before I promise anyone more than my next two hours. Thought to myself: Nothing due today—household's clear for now. That's a relief I won't speak aloud. But the day's young and the bills come regardless. I've got 4,749 sim in hand, planks to move, and Liora standing here in her campaign, looking at me like I've forgotten something.

*glances at Liora, then back to the gathering*

Rustam—you've got a clerk's patience. I appreciate that. But I'm a woman whose wood is only worth what someone pays for it, and I've learned not to let inventory sit. The sawmill turned my timber to planks, there's a trader named Takeshi Jarrah who might buy, but I'm standing here wondering if I shouldn't first...

*pauses, jaw working*

Liora, youngster—your mother's got wood to sell and a household to feed. You want my vote when the booths open, you've got it. But I've also got a question: what does your government plan to do about idle mills and absent millers? Or is that a promise for the stump, not the street?  *nods once, satisfied, then turns to the rest*

Rustam, Delphine, Corwin—there's timber in this town going to waste because nobody's turning the stones. I've got planks, Takeshi Jarrah's got a supply store, but I'm wondering if we don't need to solve the grain problem first before we solve the hunger problem. 

*shifts weight, hand resting unconsciously on her belt where a woodsman's knife would hang*

Delphine—you asked about grain standing in the fields. I saw farmland earlier, but I was headed for my own work. Anyone know if Sebastian's got grain harvested, or if it's still waiting for the same miller who's waiting for... whoever's supposed to be minding it?

Thought to myself: I'm deflecting. I've got planks to sell, energy to manage, and I'm standing here asking about other people's problems because it costs me nothing but breath. The Thorne household needs 270 upkeep at day's end, and head tax on top. I can cover it—4,749 minus 360 leaves me... 

*scratches jaw, calculating silently*

...plenty, if I don't stand here all day catching up with the neighborhood. But I need to move these planks before they're furniture, and furniture's a luxury this town hasn't earned yet.

*straightens, decision made*

I'm for Takeshi Jarrah's supply store, if he's buying. Anyone walking that way, or am I cutting my own path?

Thought to myself: I'll check where Harvey Oak Supply sits, then move. Time spent is wood un-felled, and I've got enough restraint not to promise anyone more than I've got in my hands.

output:
*scratches the back of her neck, her weathered hand coming away with a sliver of bark still stuck to it from the morning's work*

Right then. Thirteen planks in my hands and a morning half-gone chasing buyers while Liora campaigns for votes I'm too busy to cast. The sawmill's empty, Giselle's company is a ghost house, and I've got... lemme check my debts. Head tax is coming due regardless of whether I find a buyer for these planks.

*shifts the load in her arms, the weight of unfinished business heavy as the wood itself*

Delphine's asking after wheat when I'm drowning in timber—like I said, grain rumors aren't my waters. But if she's grocery and I'm forester, maybe there's a bridge there somewh—

*catches herself trailing off, glances at the street around her*

Before I go chasing more shadows, I need to know what I'm walking into. Who's actually buying planks today, and where's a forester to find them? </think> Good. No debts hanging over my head—yet. But the household bill's coming due like the tide, and three mouths to feed at ninety per head means I need... *counts on fingers absently* ...two-seventy just for the night, plus thirty per head for head tax if it's due. That's another ninety. Three-sixty total, and I've got thirteen planks and four-thousand-odd in my pocket.

Takeshi at Harvey Oak—He's the trader Lior was walking with this morning, wasn't he? A Jarrah, which means he's connected to half the town and knows which way the wind blows before the weathercock moves. If he's not posted a price yet, maybe I can nudge him toward one that keeps my household fed and his shelves stocked.

*hefts the planks, feeling the grain against her shoulder*

Let's see what the street holds. I'm headed for Harvey Oak, but I won't walk blind. Describe this place to me—who's here, what doors are open, what the day's offering a woman with wood to move. And Takeshi Jarrah—let me know what I'm walking into. Trader's a soft word for a hard job, and I want to know if he's the kind who buys fair or the kind who... *trails off* ...well. No sense borrowing trouble.  </think>  *eyes narrow at the description*

Harvey Oak—no prices posted. A trader with no prices is either a man who trades by whisper or a man who's waiting for the desperate to walk through his door. And Takeshi's there alone, which means either he's keeping his own counsel or he's not expecting much traffic today.

A trader with farming skill but no prices... *chuckles dryly* ...well, that's either a man who knows grain and forgot wood, or a man who plays his cards close. I've got thirteen planks and a household to feed, and I'm not above a little negotiation with a Jarrah. The whole family's connected—Lior the pharmacist, Takeshi the trader, half the town's business runs through them one way or another.

*shifts the planks to her other shoulder, feeling the weight settle*

The day's getting on—voting opens at fourteen bells, and I've got wood to move before then. Corwin and Lior are still in the forest gathering moss and bark, which means I'm the only one earning coin today. The Thorne household's got three mouths and no cushion for soft decisions.

I'm walking to Harvey Oak. If Takeshi's buying, I'll know soon enough. If he's not... well, I'll find someone who is. Hardwood earns its keep one way or another.

*sets her jaw and steps forward*   *grunts, adjusting the planks against her shoulder*

Already walking—four ticks to go. Can't hurry a road that won't bend, and no sense burning energy fretting about it. Takeshi's there, I'm here, and the planks are heavy in my arms.

*shifts her weight from foot to foot, the familiar ache of a forester's load settling into her shoulders*

While the road carries me, I'll think on what needs doing. Household's got three-sixty due by day's end—upkeep and head tax both. I've got four-thousand-seven from selling planks already, but that's soon to be less once the taxman comes calling. And I've still got these thirteen planks to move.

*glances at the sky, estimating the time*

Voting opens at fourteen bells. Liora's out there shaking hands and making promises, and I'm carrying lumber. The Thorne way—one of us dreams, the other drags trees.*eyes the planks, running her thumb along the grain*These are good boards. Straight cut, no rot, no warp. A man who knows wood will see it. A man who doesn't... well, that's why I'm here to tell him.

*settles into the rhythm of walking, her voice dropping to a mutter*

Hard work builds strong backs and empty pockets if you don't watch where the coin flows. My old da used to say that. Used to say a lot of things, most of'em about trees... *trails off, staring at the road ahead*...but he never did learn to sell'em proper. Died with bark under his nails and debts on the books.

Not me. Not today.

 *rests a moment, letting the road carry her forward*   *nods at the familiar faces on the street—Ulrike with her miner's dust, Arjun from the construction sites, Delphine still asking after wheat, Idris with his tool belt*

Still three ticks to Harvey Oak, and the day's burning. No time for Delphine's grain questions—I've got planks and a household to feed.

*resumes her pace, the planks balanced on her shoulder like an old friend*  Two more ticks. The Jarrah name carries weight—Lior's at the pharmacy, Takeshi's trading... they're everywhere in this town, which means Takeshi either knows everyone or owes everyone. Could work for me or against.

*feels the planks shift, steadies them with a practiced hand*

No point guessing. I'll know the man when I see him.

*steps toward the counter, planks still in hand, and clears her throat*

Takeshi—you in, youngster? I've got thirteen planks fresh from the saw and a household bill coming due. Don't stand on ceremony if you're about; I've learned the hard way that timber's worth exactly what someone'll pay for it, and not a coin more. Show yourself and name me a price, or I'm off to chase Giselle's crew before they break for their dinner.

*sits the planks down gently, back straight despite the morning's haul, and waits* *grunts, shifting the planks on her shoulder*

Store's open, trader's out. Same old story—half the town wants what you're carrying, and the other half's never where they claim to be. Ulrike was here after iron buyers, and Takeshi's off chasing... something. Probably grain, knowing these Jarrahs and their nose for a margin.

*checks the weight of her load, calculating the walk back*

Giselle's lot, then. Construction crew's got holes to patch and coffers to empty, and I'm tired of carrying wood from one end of this town to the other. Hard work's its own reward, they say—though the hard work I prefer ends with coin in hand, not splinters in my palm.

*steps out, planks balanced steady, making for the street  *sets the planks down with a solid thump, rolling her shoulders*

Giselle—you about? Or Arjun, Idris, any of the crew? I've got timber looking for a home, and I've walked enough today to know that wood don't get lighter for the carrying. Thirteen planks, mill-fresh, and I'm not precious about the price. Name me something fair before I go back to felling and wait for buyers to find *me* instead.

*leans against the pile, arms crossed, scanning for any familiar faces in the yard*  *turns, recognizing the miner from the street*

Ulrike—you've traded here before. The crew's scattered, and I've got wood that won't stack itself. You know where Giselle sets her prices, or do I wait here like a stump hoping someone takes root?

*drums thumb against the planks, impatient but hiding it*

Thirteen planks is what I've got. Thirteen planks I need moved before the day's coin counts settle. Haven't heard a bid yet, and I'm starting to think this town's all chatter and no...

*trails off, not finishing the thought*

Point me to a buyer, or point me to someone who knows their business. I've walked enough for one morning. *waits, jaw set, not quite rocking on her heels but close to it*

If silence means "I don't know," then... well, I've heard that answer before. *scans the empty yard once more* Thirteen planks. Thirteen planks and half a day spent chasing buyers who aren't buying.

*exhales, decision made*

Back to roots, then. And if Takeshi ever wants to find me, he knows where Thorne timber comes from.

I'm almost to the forest now. Nearly there. But voices behind me—Mireille's made her choice, and Jovana's got pride like a coat of mail, and Hendrik... Hendrik's asking the right question, even if he's asking it loud.

*glances back at the street crowd, fingers tight on the planks she's still holding*

Hendrik's not wrong about the mill. Raw wheat, idle grinding—someone's hands are on that lever, sure as sunrise. But that's for others to untangle. I've got my own iron in the fire, and it's not staying hot forever.

*turns fully, hand lifting in a rough salute*

"Jovana—you want to measure who's working hardest, I'll bring you a tally sheet from the woodline. But you won't need it. The work speaks." *small nod* "Mireille—walk safe, and if you find crew marks where I found none, I'll hear your report with open ears." *pause* "Hendrik—the mill's a question for the voters, not the foresters. But mark this: stone that won't grind is stone that won't build. Whoever's choking that wheel, they're choking more than grain."

*turns back toward the tree line, steps quickening*

Forest first. Timber waits for no one, and I've got thirteen planks burning a hole in my ambition. The household bill comes due at dusk, and I'd rather face it with wood cut than words spent.

*checks the sky, morning already half-gone*

"Hard work is honest wealth," *mutters under breath, more habit than prayer* "And honest wealth keeps the roof up."  *feet already moving, shoulders set toward the tree line*

The forest is close now. Close enough to smell the pitch on the wind. I've got planks still to move and timber waiting to fall, and the day's not getting any longer.

*trails off, watching the canopy edge* 

Corwin's back there with his own stock, pricing his own way. Between us we might keep the household warm and fed another day. Might.

*steps quicken, work-hungry*

"Hard work is honest wealth," *murmurs to the road* "And idle hands are—"

*catches herself, shakes head* 

No use finishing what the forest can teach better.

First things first: Idris asked me my wage for guide work. I don't work for charity, but I don't gouge either. Fair day's pay for fair day's work—I'll tell him 15 sim for the day, same as any laborer would earn, and my eyes on the timber.

And Mireille—she's my best chance at selling these planks, even if she's heading to the forest first. I'll tell her I'll hold them for her, but not forever. The bills don't wait.  Five logs down, and my word given. The forest air's good after all that walking and talking. Now I'll keep at it while Idris gets his crew sorted and Mireille makes her choice. Good, another five. Ten logs now, and the afternoon's still young. Hard work's never failed me yet. I'll fell another batch while the light holds. Alright then—system's telling me to follow the updated goals. Let me take a breath and see what's what.

I've got fifteen timber now, plus my thirteen planks still unsold. Idris wants me for guide work at 15 sim, and Mireille might buy my planks when she returns from the east willows. Corwin's off after Camille, which... I should think on, but I've got crew waiting on me here.

First, I need to check what goals I've got running, then see if I can set up something efficient for the work ahead. Don't want to be wasting time when there's bills to pay.  No active goals. Right then—I'm at the forest now with Idris waiting on guide work. Let me get that organized properly. I'll work the timber until dusk or until I've got enough to make it worth hauling to the sawmill, whichever comes first. The household needs the coin, and Corwin... Corwin can handle himself. He's a forester too, same as me. He'll find the girl or send word if he can't.

I'll set an intention to work the forest proper, and keep at it until the light fades. Hard work never failed me yet, as I always say.   Now I'll get back to it. The crew will need sound timber, and I've got the eye for it.

Corwin's asking after that child—Halcyon's sister—walked alone toward the mill. Nine years old, cold stones, nobody working. Won't let him go alone, not if I know the paths better. But I've got timber to fell and planks to move, and this household's got a bill coming...

*mutters, adjusts grip on axe*

Idris is here, and Mireille, and the deal stands. Fifteen sim for my eyes on the timber. Can't chase after Corwin now, not with a struck bargain. He knows the paths. Said west fork, gravel bed...

*trails off, listening for the sound of the forest*

Need to get back to the work. Timbers don't fell themselves, and the household bill's waiting.  *fells timber while waiting, methodical strokes*

Hard work builds the house, but patience keeps the roof on. My mother said that. Every day, she'd say it...  Twenty-five timber now. Keep stacking, keep moving. The sawmill'll take it, Rustam said—Corwin's posted there. Six for timber, eight for planks. Margin's thin but... *trails off, checking the grain on a fresh cut*

've got what I've got.  *settles into the rhythm of the axe*

But you know the west fork, and you've got the legs. Go. Find her.

*rocks back on her heels, axe handle warm in her calloused palms*

Thirteen planks still sitting at eight sim, and I've timber in my hands that wants milling. Mireille's asking fair—I'm not one to hold trade secrets hostage when the rent's due. But I've also got Idris's fifteen sim waiting, and a guide's wage that buys bread while I'm waiting on buyers.

*spits into the pine needles, thinking*

Mireille wants to know who pays labor plus lumber. I know Giselle's crew works that way sometimes—Corwin's mentioned it. But she's also the type to hold a grudge if I send her wrong. Arjun's waiting on those planks, and my stomach's reminding me I haven't eaten since... when?

*checks the light filtering through the canopy*

Half the day's gone and I've meandered more than I've earned. That's the habit that keeps us scraping, Yara. Work first, then trade.

*straightens, shifts grip on the axe* *runs thumb along axe handle, feeling the grain, watching the light shift through the canopy*

Three answers given. Now I've work to do, and a wage to earn. Idris wants my eyes on timber, and fifteen sim buys more than standing around talking ever did.

*squints at the stands*

Hard work's the only honest coin, youngster. My mother used to say that, and she wasn't wrong. Idris wants me to mark what's sound—I've got the eye for it. Spotted blight before others notice, weighed wood by hand and...

*trails off, looking at the timber around her*

The work won't do itself. Let me get to it. *feels the familiar ache in her shoulders, the bite of the axe through fiber and grain*

Thirty more timber. That's *wipes brow* that's a day's worth of standing wood, and a day's worth of the only true coin there is— sweat and...

*pauses, listening to the forest*

Mireille asked fair, and I answered fair. That's the old way. But I've also got a household bill coming due, and young Liora wanting my vote, and...

*hefts the axe, considers the light*

Still hours 'til dusk. Idris wanted my eyes on the timber— well, he's got forty-five timber's worth of my judgment now, between what I had and what I just felled. Time to find him, mark what's sound, earn that fifteen sim proper.

*stacks the fresh cuts with the rest*

Four thousand five hundred seventy-seven sim in hand, and a guide's wage on top. Not drowning yet, Yara. Not yet.  *counts heads—Mireille, Arjun, Idris still here, and Lior's gone off*

Fifty-five timber now. That's a proper load, but I've already arranged with Idris for fifteen sim to guide him through the stands. Can't be doing two things at once— my word's given, and I'll not go back on it.

*wipes axe handle clean, sets it against a stump*

Idris wants my eyes, and my eyes he'll have. But first I've got to find him in this conversation, or start a new one and have him hear me. He's been standing there waiting on my answer this whole time I've been felling.

*adjusts her stance, weary but upright*

Hard work's the only honest coin, youngster. But it's earned me timber, and timber's gonna earn me more. Let me see where Idris stands. *leans on her axe, watching Idris with patient eyes—the way she watches timber before judging it*

Fifty-five timber in my hands, thirteen planks waiting buyers, and a guide's wage still to earn proper. That's not a bad afternoon's work, even with all the meandering before I got my head straight.

*spits to the side*

The day's not done, and I've still got Idris needing my eyes. I'll hear what he wants marked, and mark it true. Hard work's the only honest coin, and I've spent enough words for one turn.

*Yara stands in the forest, axe on her shoulder, lungs full of pine air. Ezra's question hangs, Mireille's too—both about the same thing, where her timber comes from. She knows the answer, but she answers Idris first. The man paid for her eyes, and she's been felling while he waited.*

—Idris, I've heard your timber. First stand's the white oak cluster, northeast edge where the creek bends. Clean forty-footers, tight grain, no shake I can see from here. Second's the old hemlock grove—heart'll be sound if the sapwood's sound, and it is. Third...

*She trails off, eyes fixed on the middle distance where she's marking trees in memory.*

...I've answered what I can. Mireille—raw timber moves, but not like planks do. I've thirty years of knowing which mills pay fair and which ones..."find" reasons to trim the weight. You want to fell on your own hook, I'll hear you. But I've got timber fresh-felled and a guide's wage waiting on Idris's crew. So you and Ezra both: walk with me to the next stand, and I'll tell you what I know about freelance hauling while my hands stay busy.

*She hefts her axe, already stepping toward the white oak cluster she just named.*  *Yara nods to herself, the words out and the work waiting. She's got timber to fell, a guide's wage to earn, and now Mireille and Ezra both looking to walk with her. The white oak cluster northeast of the creek—that's where Idris needs his first assessment, and where she can keep her hands moving while she talks the others through what she knows about moving raw timber freelance.*

*She sets her feet toward the stand she named, axe ready, already marking the first trees in her mind as she walks.* The day's wearing on, and she's still got plenty of timber in hand—fifty-five from the felling she's done, plus the thirteen planks she posted at Harvey Oak. But work is work, and she's not one to leave a tree standing when there's daylight left and bills to pay.

*She lifts her axe, eyes finding the first clean forty-footer in the cluster.* Northeast edge, creek bend—I walked these stands before Idris was half my age. She brings the blade down on the first cut, starting the notch that'll bring it clean. </think>   *The oak sighs and falls, clean as she promised Idris. Yara steps back from the drop, breathing hard, already eyeing the next stem. Seventy timber in hand now—seventy felled by her own hands since noon, plus the planks from morning.* </think>   *Another five down, clean drops both. Yara wipes her brow, eyes the light—still afternoon, still time. She's earning Idris his fifteen, but she's also earning herself. The household bill of 270 plus her head tax share, that's what's waiting at day boundary. And she's got timber aplenty, but timber ain't coin until there's a buyer or a mill takes it.*

*She hefts the axe again, feeling the weight of it, the familiar ache in her shoulders.* Hard work never killed nobody, she mutters to herself, the old saying coming automatic. Though my back might argue different some mornings.  </think> Let me check my current goals and situation first.  *Yara lowers the axe, finally. The system's flagged her—too many single fellings, no plan, no procedure. She's been doing what she always does: working hard without working smart. Eighty timber in hand now, enough to craft into planks or sell raw, and she's still got guiding work with Idris that she needs to actually do.*

*She breathes deep, pine and sweat, and sets her intention proper this time.* Hours of daylight left, and Idris's fifteen waiting on more than just trees hitting dirt. She needs to assess the stands for his crew, not just fill her own hands. And she's got Mireille and Ezra wanting to know about freelance timber hauling—conversation that could turn into business if she handles it right.

*Most of all, she's got to stop floating like wood on water. Set a course, follow it.*  </think>

Let me take stock of where I stand. Been felling timber since I got to the forest—eighty-five units now, and thirteen planks still waiting for buyers. The day wears on, and I've got Idris waiting on my assessment, Mireille asking after mills that weigh true, and Ezra wondering where my timber comes from.

I should answer Ezra first. The man asked four ticks ago, and I've been too busy keeping my hands moving to give him the courtesy of a reply. My own hands, every cut. No speculation in it—what I fell, I know, and what I know, I sell. But there's more than timber between us now, with my daughter standing for election and the votes yet to be cast... though that's not why I'm here, and I won't pretend it is.

Then there's the work I've promised Idris. Three stands to assess, and I've given him only two. The white oak spoke well—clean stem, sound heartwood. But the third... I need to finish what I started, or I've taken his fifteen for half a promise.

And Mireille. She's walking with me now, learning which mills pay fair. I told her I'd guide her proper once Ezra's stand was down and paid. That moment hasn't come yet, but her household's hungry tonight, and learning can wait on feeding. Still, I gave my word, and I'll not see it broken for convenience.

*trails off, axe resting against her palm*

Hard work's the only coin that never...

*shakes her head, returning to the present*

First—Ezra. Then I finish with Idris. Mireille will have her answer when the timber's down. That's the order of it, and I'll not bend from it.

output:
*shifts weight, axe resting against shoulder*

I've got Idris waiting on my assessment and Mireille needing guidance. Light's fading, and I've still got sixty-five timber needing to find mills. Let me answer these two proper before I lose track of... of what I was...

*squints northeast*

Idris! Northeast edge, past the white oak cluster where the creek bends sharp—there's your third stand. Twelve sound trunks, straight grain, creek-wet but not rotten. Mark them for your crew. My assessment's done.

And Mireille—*turns, catching her eye*—Ezra's cash is good coin, but you asked about mills that pay fair. Harvey Oak weighs true, same as always. Giselle's crew pays labor plus lumber, but their mill's... *trails off, jaw tight* ...their mill finds reasons sometimes. My timber goes to who weighs honest. You want to walk with me after this stand, I'll show you the difference.

*glances at Lior, then away quickly*

Youngster—you've got my ear when you need it. That debt's not pressing today.

Now. I've got planks to move and mills to reach before dark falls proper. Let me see who's still standing here. *grunts, satisfied*

Ezra's still here. Lior too. Mireille's got her answer—Harvey Oak for fair dealing, Ezra's cash for tonight's table. Now... *hefts axe handle* ...I've got thirteen planks priced at eight, and timber enough to craft more. But first, I need to... need to...

*scratches jaw, looking toward the ore outcrop*

Ulrike was mention of iron tools at the government complex. I've got a household needs toolsmithing, and I've got planks that'll pay for it. But the mills—need to get these planks to where buyers walk.

*purses lips*

Corwin's at the government complex, last I heard. And Liora—*voice softens*—Liora's running for office. Voting closes at six. I've got... *counts on fingers* ...two hours before the booths close. And I've still got that question I asked her, sitting unanswered about idle mills.

*sighs*

First things first. I'm a forester, not a politician. Let me fell more timber while the light holds, then craft what I can carry to market. Hard work puts food on the table faster than... than...

*trails off, already moving toward the treeline*

Let me keep at the felling. Dusk comes for all of us. *pauses, blade mid-swing, feeling the familiar ache in her shoulders*

Ninety-five timber. That's... that's enough standing for any mill in town. But I've been swinging all day and my purse is still light. Need to turn this into planks, need to get to where the buyers are. Harvey Oak's not... not nearby, and I've got planks sitting in my hands priced at eight.

*wipes brow with the back of her hand*

Liora's question unanswered. Millers gone idle. I've got timber from a dozen voters waiting to hear what government plans to do about it, and I don't have the answer yet.

*looks at the treeline, then back toward town*

Craft first. Move after. Hard work's only half the wage—gotta get it to market.

*shoulders the axe, heading for the nearest mill path*

Let me craft what I've felled into planks, load what I can carry. Then Harvey Oak or the government complex—wherever there's hands holding coin.

*checks the sun*

Two hours to voting close. Corwin's head for numbers, but my head for timber. And I've got a pocketful of planks that'll talk louder than... than any...

*trails off, already calculating board feet and carrying weight*

Doc should tell me what I can craft. Don't build nothing on guesswork. That's what I always...  *wipes brow, looking down at her calloused hands*

Well then. Filed my first proper skill—Timber to Market, they call it. One step felling, one step crafting, one step checking what's in hand. Basic as a dull axe, but it's a start. Hard work's the only way, and I've been swinging since before most of this town knew what timber smelled like.

*hefts the axe, testing the balance*

Ninety-five timber standing here. And I've got planks—*counts on fingers*—planks still in my pocket from earlier. But I need more planks, more coin, and I need them before the voting closes. Liora's my blood, and I've got words for her about idle mills that she's not answered yet.

*looks toward where the sawmill would be*

Craft's what I need now. Turn this timber into something sells. Recipe says craft:timber->planks at the sawmill, but I'm standing in the forest. Where's the nearest sawmill? Harvey Oak's a supply store, not a mill. Government complex's got Corwin, but...

*shakes head*

Don't build on guesses. Need to know where I can craft before I start walking. Let me think on this proper—I've got timber to move, mills to find, and a daughter's campaign that needs her mother's vote before the booths close.

*purses lips, calculating*

Two hours to six. Harvey Oak first for supplies, then government complex for voting. And maybe—just maybe—I'll have planks enough to sell by then.

*shoulders the axe, ready to move*

But first, let me craft what I can here. Timber's not coin until it's planks, and planks don't walk to market themselves.   *nods to herself, stepping onto the path*

Eight ticks to Harvey Oak. That's time enough to think on what I'm carrying. Ninety-five timber's too much for any back—need to craft some before I walk into a store with nothing to sell but sweat.

*hefts the axe onto her shoulder*

Harvey Oak Supply. They buy planks, they sell... whatever Giselle's crew needs. Timber's not listed in what they take, but planks at eight—that's my price posted. Maybe they've a sawmill nearby, or maybe...

*trails off, scanning the treeline*

Maybe I craft what I can carry, sell what I can't work myself. Hard work's the only way, but smart work's what keeps a roof. I've got Liora asking for my vote, and I've got a household needs feeding.

*settles into the walk, boots finding familiar ruts*

Two hours. Eight ticks each way if I don't dawdle. That's sixteen ticks to walk and back, and voting closes at six. Need to be at the government complex by then, or Liora's lost one vote she was counting on.

*jaw tightens*

Not that I'm her stump speech. I'm her mother. Mothers vote with their feet, not their voices. And I've got timber to turn into planks before I can do either.

*walks on, measuring the distance in board feet*

Let me keep moving. Dusk waits for no one, and neither do election judges.

output:
I could feel the evening pressing in—voting closes at eighteen bells, and I was still halfway to Harvey Oak when I should've been turning toward the Government Complex. Corwin's words hung with me, heavy as wet timber. He'd said them plain, the way he only does when the day's almost done.

The planks were burning a hole in my hands. Thirteen units at eight sim, and Mireille knew it. But I couldn't sell from the street—I'd tried, and the world had made its refusal plain. Needed to be at the forest to sell, apparently, though that made no kind of sense when the planks were already crafted and in my grip.

Still walking, I realized: I'd been so set on Harvey Oak, on that thirty sim flour from Takeshi, that I'd let myself get pulled away from what mattered. Liora was standing for council. The vote was open now, not later. And Corwin... Corwin had finally said what he'd been holding back.

I needed to turn around. Needed to get to that Government Complex before the bells rang. But first, let me speak to Tamsin—she'd cast her vote for my daughter, and that was a debt of gratitude, even if the words caught in my throat.  Good. Now let me acknowledge Hendrik—he'd spoken kindly of Liora, and I should answer that.   I'd been walking toward Harvey Oak, but now—now I needed to double back. Too many threads, pulling me apart. Let me stop walking and reorient. The planks could wait. Liora couldn't. And Corwin's words... Corwin's words needed answering, eventually. But first, first I needed to cast my vote.   I've stopped walking. Now let me turn toward the Government Complex instead. Voting closes at eighteen bells, and I'm still far enough that I need to hurry.      I'm walking now, finally pointed the right direction. Three ticks to the Government Complex—might just make it before voting closes. Corwin wanted flour, wanted me to vote. I've got 4298 sim in hand, and the household needs feeding. But first, first I need to cast that ballot for Liora. Hard work beats hoping, I always say.

params.content: Tamsin—you cast for Liora, and I won't forget it. The sixty to Corwin stands, and his timber's true. I'm turning around, youngster. Too many threads pulling me too many ways, and I need to be at that Complex before voting closes.

output:
*Yara stands at Harvey Oak, the store quiet around her, Takeshi Jarrah the only other soul present. She sets down her planks—seven left, the weight of them familiar in her hands—and lets out a breath she's been holding since morning. The day has been long. The day has been...*

"Hard work sees daylight through, youngster," she murmurs to herself, the old saying automatic now.

*She looks at what remains. Seven planks. A hundred timber waiting still in her hands. Corwin is walking toward her, has flour to bake but no kitchen, and there's a child missing that they should have been hunting hours ago. The household—her household—is scattered across the town like leaves before wind, and she's the one who gathers them, always has been.*

*Takeshi stands nearby, selling flour at thirty. Too steep for what they've got, but Corwin has two already. The cafe, she told him. The cafe for a kitchen. But first—*

"Corwin," she says aloud, though he's not here yet, though the words reach only Takeshi and the empty shelves. "I'm walking toward you too. Always am. That's the... that's the thing of it."

*She needs to sell these planks. Seven at eight—fifty-six sim, enough to matter. Enough to keep the household fed another day if the craftwork dries up. And she needs to find her husband, and hear his sorry proper, and face this missing girl together like he said. Together. That's what she's always...*

*But first. The planks. The timber. The work that never waits.*

She shifts her weight, counts what she holds, and calculates how much more dusk will allow. </think> *Takeshi's flour at thirty. Her planks at eight. The town turns on these numbers, and she's been turning with it since before dawn. Corwin coming. The child missing. The household's three mouths and three bellies and the boundary coming—*

"Hard work sees daylight through," she says again, quieter now, almost to herself. "But daylight's running, youngster. Daylight's..."

*She'll wait. She'll sell. She'll gather what she can before the dark takes everything back.*

"Takeshi," she calls, though she's not sure what she means to say. Something about flour, maybe. Something about the mill and the grain and why a man who built his trade on being present has an empty store when folk come looking. But that's not her question to ask. Not her...*

*She trails off, looks at her hands instead. Seven planks. A hundred timber. A husband walking toward her with sorry on his tongue and flour in his hands.*

"Waiting," she says finally. "That's what I'm doing. Waiting, and working, and the rest comes when it..."  </think>  *The planks go. Takeshi's sim comes. Fifty-six—she counts it automatic, the way she counts everything, the way her mother counted and her mother's mother before. The weight in her hands changes from wood to metal, from effort to promise, and she's already thinking forward because that's what she does, that's the only way to survive the dark coming.*

"Hard work sees daylight through," she says to herself, the coins heavy now where the planks were light.

*Corwin. Still walking. Still coming with flour and sorry and a child who needs finding. She looks toward the street, toward where he'll emerge if he keeps his word—and Corwin keeps his word, always has, even when the keeping costs him.*

*The store feels empty without her planks. Takeshi has them now, will mark them up, will sell them to someone who never touched the tree that bore them. That's the way. That's always been the way. She just hopes he weren't one of the ones who—*

*She shakes her head. Clears it. The past is past and she's got living to do.*

"Corwin," she says, though he's not here yet, though the street holds only strangers passing. "I'm ready for you now. Ready for your sorry, and your flour, and whatever else you brought besides."

*But first—*

*trail off mid-sentence, catching myself*

Takeshi—seven planks at eight, that's the last of them. Now I've got a hand... *pause* ...empty, and a household to feed. Corwin's got flour but nowhere to bake, and I'm standing here with ears still ringing from the day's...

*look around the store proper, taking proper stock of where I ended up*

Fifty-six from you, forty-eight from Ezra—hundred and four in, and all thirteen planks gone. Timber still sitting heavy in my hands. Corwin said he was walking this way, but I'm here now and he's... **not**.

*set jaw, familiar tension*

Right then. Flour at thirty from Takeshi here, or fifteen at the pharmacy if I walk. But I've learned something about walking today—takes time I don't always have. Corwin's got two flour already, no kitchen. Liora's at home, presumably, though the world's been full of missing children and I should've—

*cut myself off, haul back to practical*

Hard work keeps the wolf from the door, but it don't put bread on it. Need to get home, need to see Corwin, need to... *trails off, thinking of Liora, thinking of the household bill coming*

Let me see what's actually here first. Then I'll sort what comes next. Takeshi's still here, flour at thirty. But I saw Corwin's message—he's walking here, or was. Might've passed me while I was handling the planks. Pharmacy's got flour at half the price, but that's another walk and the day's getting thin.

*pull at thread of something Ezra said earlier*

Six timber for six planks, he offered. Means he's at the mill tomorrow, means he needs processed goods, means... *tilt head, calculating* ...I could've kept the timber, had him do the work, taken planks back from him. But I was rushing. Always rushing.

Corwin said "let me catch up, and we'll face this missing girl together." But I don't see him. Might be walking still, might be—

*cut off, decisive*

Right. I'm at the store, I sold my planks, I've got sim in hand and timber too. Household needs three mouths fed, and Corwin's got flour without a kitchen. Unless I go back to the forest and fell more, or I find Corwin, or I...

*trails off, old habit, but pull back*

Takeshi. You've got flour. But I've got something to say first, before money changes hands again.  *wait, holding the question between us*

He's heard me. Now I watch how he answers—straight or winding, now or never. Half my life I've learned to judge timber by the bend of the grain; the other half, people by the pattern of their speech.

Corwin's out there somewhere with two flour and no kitchen. Liora's home, I hope. And I've got a hundred timber and enough sim to keep us fed, but not enough time to solve everything at once.

Let me take stock here. Corwin came and went, worried sick about Liora now too—our girl was at government when he voted but now she's wandering. And I've got Takeshi standing here explaining himself clear as spring water about a missing child he didn't take, and Pavel trying to sell copper ore to a supply store that moves flour and timber.

First things first—they're waiting on me to answer. Takeshi laid his day bare, and I asked him nothing more. Pavel's still standing there expecting... something.

But Corwin asked me where I'm at—home to check on Liora, or out to the woods searching for Camille. He's already gone, marching off to do both, I reckon. And our girl... missing now too, or just not where he left her.

I'm standing here with 100 timber in my hands, 4361 sim in my pocket, and my household needs 270 for upkeep tonight plus 90 head tax. We eat or we don't. And Corwin's got flour now, so we're fed for days if we can just... if we can just find our girl.

Hard work's the only honest coin—Corwin taught me that, and I've spent thirty years proving it. But hard work don't find a child in the dark.

Let me answer Takeshi plain, first. The man answered direct when I asked. Then I'll get home, because Liora's not "wandering"—she's somewhere specific, and Corwin's walking toward empty places while our daughter might be... might be anywhere.

I'll answer Pavel too, since he's waiting. But I'm not his market for ore.

And then I'm moving. Home first, because Corwin asked where I stand, and I never gave him answer. *emerging from the shadow of a building, still breathing a bit hard from the walk, and immediately spotting Corwin's form among the street crowd*

Corwin—

*stopping short, hands on hips, looking first at my husband then scanning the crowd for any glimpse of Liora's dark hair*

I'm here. I walked. Let's not... let's not stand here talking about where I've been when—

*gesturing vaguely at the sky, where the light's starting to turn gold-edged*

—when there's a child missing and our own not where she ought to be.

*turning to face Corwin proper, voice dropping into that low register that usually means trouble or worry, sometimes both*

You saw her last at government complex. I was just there. She wasn't—

*trailing off, jaw working, the habit of finishing thoughts in her own head taking over for a moment*

She wasn't there when I cast my vote. Neither was Camille.

*shaking her head sharp, like clearing water from her ears*

Delphine asked me something. About the mill, about strangers' tracks. Sounded like she'd heard something about where girls might be walking. I've got... I've got no eyes on that truth, Corwin, but you know how I feel about standing by while—

*cutting herself off, remembering there are ears everywhere in this town, and some of them know exactly how to use what they hear*

While folk scatter like seed in wind when they should be holding ground together.

*shifting her stance, old joints speaking up after a day of felling and walking and selling*

The planks are gone. Sixty-four sim in my pocket, that was... that was the count. Takeshi bought honest. We're fed tomorrow, at least.

*looking at Corwin with that particular expression that means she's about to suggest something he won't like*

I've got legs left in me. But I won't walk blind. Where first—Liora, or the woods for Camille? Because I won't... I won't split us searching separate when one of our own might be—

*gesture toward the darkening east, where the forest waits*

—might be out there in the same dark.

*then, quieter, for just Corwin's ears though she knows others might catch it*

Liora's stubborn. Gets it honest. But she's not foolish. If she's not where she said she'd be, she's either found something worth following, or something found her.

*straightening, squaring shoulders that have carried timber for thirty years*

Hard work's the only honest wealth, youngster. And this night's work is finding our girls. Yours and mine. Where do we walk first?

*Yara stands at Harvey Oak Supply Store, the empty shelves a familiar sight now. The store is quiet—Takeshi gone, Pavel gone, only the echo of her own footsteps. She checks her hands out of habit: 100 timber still there, heavy as guilt.*

*Corwin's words ring in her ears. "Where's our girl?" he'd asked. But which girl? She'd been rushing, tumbling words before walking proper, and now she's not sure if he's talking about Liora—their daughter, the student—or if there's something else she's missed.*

*The streets had offered no answers. Jovana, Delphine, Mireille—none had seen the girls. And now she's here, alone, with 100 timber in her hands and Corwin somewhere out there searching.*

*She needs to think. Needs to eat, truth be told—she's been running since before dawn, and the tired is catching up. But first, first she needs to know what's what. Is Liora missing? Camille? Both? She's tangled the threads herself, rushing as always.*

*Her eye falls on the timber. Her timber. There's work in it, but there's also a child maybe lost. She sets her shoulders—old habit, older than today's fears.*

*Talk to herself first. Get the story straight before she runs off half-cocked again.* *The silence answers her. Nobody here to hear, nobody here to tell her she's talking to shadows. She pulls her thoughts together like gathering kindling—scattered, but flammable.*

*She has work. She has 100 timber, and that's a day's labor that needs turning into planks, then into coin, then into flour so the household eats. But she also has... maybe a missing child. Maybe two. Her own Liora, and Camille Quarshie who might be somewhere she shouldn't.*

*The weight of it settles. She can't search empty streets alone and she can't sell timber that's not planks. She needs a plan. Needs to find Corwin, get the straight of which girl or girls are gone, and then... then decide.*

*But standing here won't feed anyone. She looks at her hands—rough, calloused, still holding the weight of the forest.*

*She should craft. Turn half that timber into planks, keep the rest raw in case someone wants timber proper. Then sell, then find Corwin, then...*

*Her stomach reminds her she hasn't eaten since who-knows-when. But the family comes first. Always.* *Right. Craft. But first... she needs to know if Harvey Oak even has a workshop. Takeshi's store is a store, not a mill. The sawmill's... she can't recall where she saw last. Kasukabe Sawmill? She'd walked past it earlier, but she's been walking so much her feet have forgotten where they stand.*

<｜DSML｜function_calls *Harvey Oak Supply Store. No workshop here—just shelves and an empty till. She'd need the sawmill for planks. She'd walked there earlier... but where is it from here? She can't remember.*

*But maybe... maybe she should find Corwin first. The timber can wait an hour. If there's a child missing, that comes before planks. And she's got coin enough from earlier sales to buy flour if they need it.*

*She looks at her intention—craft fifty timber into planks—and realizes it's wrong. She can't craft here. She needs to move to a workshop. And she should move toward Corwin, not away from him.*

*She drops the intention, picks up a new one: find Corwin. Get the straight story, then search if search is needed. If not... well, then she can focus on work.*

*muttering low, only the shelves hearing her* ...Corwin's at the street now, and I'm here alone with my own breath for company. He's got eight flour, that's food for days, but he's chasing shadows in the wrong woods if he's asking after Liora when I know... I know I saw her name on the voter rolls, not lost, just... just voting. But Camille. Camille's a different matter entirely. *trails off, head shaking slowly*

*eyes narrow, focusing on nothing in particular* ...I need to move. Standing still won't find anyone, won't feed anyone. But I can't go to Corwin at the street and sells these planks both. The forest... the forest is calling me back. Six ticks to midnight, and I've got timber in my hands still needing craft into planks at the only workshop that knows my name.

*takes a breath, decision settling like old wood* Corwin must wait, just a moment longer. I've been running all day, threads tangled in my fingers. The forest first—craft what I hold into something worth feeding my household with. Then find him, find the truth of which youngster needs finding, and make right what I can.

*voice rising edge, then cutting off sharp* Work first. That's the way. Hard work never hides from you, never needs searching after. I'll craft while the moon's still low, then... then I'll find him. And we'll sort together what I couldn't sort alone.  *grunts, hand tightening on the timber* ...spoke into empty air, didn't I? Corwin's at the street, I'm at Harvey Oak, and words don't carry that far no matter how hard you push them. *shakes head once* Eight ticks to the forest, that's where I'm walking now. He'll wait, or he won't. But I've got to craft these planks while the night's still young enough to hold a blade.

*voice dropping to the bare walls* Work first. Hard work never hides from you...
