*breath catching, realizing the day's almost spent and the household needs tending*

Corwin's got thirteen timber standing at street—means he's working, not waiting. Liora's got ears on her father, good. And that seventy sim work... Idris isn't false, but thirteen's still thirteen.

Election closes in forty ticks. I'm nowhere near the Government Complex, and I've got timber in hand that won't craft itself into planks before dusk.

*felling axe heavy in her palm*

Right then. Wood first, votes later if the road allows. Or... never mind. The work's what matters. The work's always what matters.

*fell_timber*—need the raw before I can make anything worth selling. Then *move* to sawmill, *craft* what I can before the light goes. Ration Bakery wants flour, not planks, but someone's always building in this town.

*taste of leathered palms, familiar ache in the shoulders*

Youngster asked me about hard work once. Told her: the forest doesn't care if you're tired. The forest only cares if you show up.

*trailing off, checking the angle of the sun*

Showed up. That's... that's what I can promise. Everything else walks on its own. *axe biting wood, the familiar rhythm of fell, drag, stack*

Two more. That's five timber in hand now—no, wait. *counts on callused fingers* Three, plus what I felled. The head gets fogged when the day's long.

*trudging to sawmill, boots heavy with forest dirt*

Crafted three planks. Three planks at... what, eight each? That's twenty-four if I find a buyer. Hendrik's already walked with his thirty-four. Arjun took six for fifty, which is... *scratches head* ...more than eight each, isn't he? Youngster paid premium, or I miscounted. Doesn't matter. Coin's coin.

*blade screaming through timber, three more boards*

Hendrik Whitlock's standing for election. Hendrik Petrov too—same name, different hands. Government's a distant thing, like weather. You notice when it ruins the crop.

*checking the light, calculating*

Still holding timber. Still need to make the household whole. Corwin's at street with thirteen of his own, and Liora's... somewhere with questions about work and worth.

*trailing off, the thought turning private—*

...told her hard work's all there is. Told her that this morning, tell myself every day. Sometimes wonder if it's just... if it's just what we say so the axe keeps lifting.

*spitting into the sawdust*

Nonsense. Wood rots slow and business sleeps light. Someone said that. Someone... right. Hendrik. Before he walked.

*shouldering what's left, ready to move again*

*standing at the street, surrounded by people, eyes scanning each face as they speak*

Corwin's saying Camille was at the temple... but Halcyon's saying she's at the mill, safe. Two different stories, and I need to know which is true before I chase ghosts. Corwin's worried about Esme still out there. Two children, or one, or none missing—depends on who's telling it straight.

Hendrik Whitlock answered me after twenty-six ticks. Small shadows moving, he says. Not gossip, just what he saw. College keeps his daylight, street keeps his dusk. He's holding wheat at eight, standing right here with Camille buying it at that same price.

*trails off, looking toward Camille*

If Camille's buying wheat... she can't be at the mill learning trade with Esme. Unless Halcyon means something else by "at the mill." Or unless Corwin saw wrong, or Halcyon's covering, or...

*shakes head slightly*

Bram's promise matters—ore-puller keeping eyes open. Halcyon's sorry came late but real. The girls are tangled up in something, even if it's just their own walking loose.

*turns attention back to the immediate*

I'm holding planks, they're worth more as shelves than in my hands, and I need timber to keep the saw moving. Corwin's got timber at six, same as before. I was going to buy eight from him at the forest, walked before closing. Then Idris was there but I didn't stop to trade, and...

*pauses, hand half-raised as if to call out, then stops*

I need to answer Bram first. He made me a promise, not a courtesy. That's the kind that binds. *mutters under breath, fist tightening*

Connection's thin. Words not reaching. But I'm still standing, still thinking. Corwin's here, Hendrik's here, Halcyon's here. Need to sort what's real from what's worry.

If Camille's buying wheat from Hendrik Whitlock right now, then Halcyon's "at the mill learning trade with Esme" doesn't hold. Unless he means she was there, walked here. Timeline matters. Children moving fast.

*looks around again, noting who's actually present*

I'll try Hendrik Whitlock direct. He answered once, he'll answer again if I can reach him. Question is whether I ask about wheat or about shadows. He said he's not one to gossip—but he saw something.  *jaw tightens, frustration flickering, then settles*

Tools aren't reaching. But I'm still here, still holding planks, still with people who can speak. I'll work with what I have. Look around, take stock, move when I can.

The market list says I've got planks at eight, standing right here. Eleven planks. Corwin's got timber at six, nineteen sticks. I need raw material—can't craft without timber, and I've got none in hand. The sawmill work's stopped until I feed it.

*considers*

Hendrik Petrov was at the sawmill earlier, bought my planks at three-twenty. Then I was going to get timber from Corwin, walked to forest, found Idris there instead of Corwin. Spoke to Idris about missing girls. Walked back with only three timber in hand, crafted to planks, tried to sell more... then Corwin appeared with flour.

Timeline's tangled. But the work is simple: fell timber, craft planks, sell for profit. Missing girls matter, but bread matters too. Household needs eating.

*decision firms*

I'll look around, see what's actually happening where I stand. Then move if the connection holds. *hands flexing at her sides, steadying herself against the thinness in the air*

Connection's failing. Every call dropping into fog. But I'm still here—Yara Thorne, forester, standing on street with planks in hand and people around me. The physics don't change just because the tools won't answer.

*reciting under her breath like a prayer*

"Hard work's the only coin that never devalues. Hard work's the only coin..."

*reviews what she knows*

Camille Quarshie: buying wheat at eight, standing right here. Halcyon said she's at mill learning trade with Esme. Corwin said she's at temple buying wheat alone. Two stories, three locations. Someone's wrong or everyone's moving fast.

Hendrik Whitlock: selling wheat at eight, saw small shadows moving at mill. Not gossip, just witness.

Corwin: selling flour at fifteen, timber at six. Was at forest earlier, now here.

Bram: at outcrop pulling ore, no small feet seen, promised eyes open walking home.

Mireille: construction, was with us on street earlier.

Idris: was at forest when I walked there, spoke about missing girls.

My inventory: planks 11. Need timber to keep working. Need to eat eventually—household's got Liora and Corwin, both counting on upkeep.

Election: day 2, candidacy closes 10:00, voting 14:00-18:00. Nobody declared yet.

*mouth tightens, decision forming*

If tools won't reach, I'll act within myself. Set my intention clear, hold it until the world returns. The work never stops just because the path's obscured.

I'm buying timber from Corwin. Eight at six, what I meant to do at forest. Then craft, then sell, then home to check on Liora. The girls... I asked. Bram promised. If something's real, it'll surface.

*touches the planks in her hand like talismans*

Eleven planks. Eleven chances to sell, to eat, to keep the household standing. Money's just a tool. Hard work's the only coin...

*clutches the 11 planks like they might sprout wings and fly*

Ezra Lund's got planks at seven at the mill, and I'm posting eight here on the street. Course he is. Course I am. That's... that's how it goes, isn't it. Undercut or be undercut, and I never was quick at the arithmetic of...

*looks at the crowd gathered here - Halcyon standing with news of his sister, Corwin with his questions about Esme and Liora and government seats, a whole conversation about milling and elections swirling*

First things first. Halcyon's standing there with word about Camille, and I asked after her like she was lost when she wasn't. Need to... to set that straight. And Corwin—he's heard Liora talking government work, which I told her to keep close until she understood what she was buying into. But thirteen-year-olds don't keep close what shines, do they. None of us did, at that age.

*takes a breath, shoulders straightening*

Hard work keeps the hands honest, even when the tongue's still learning.

*turns to face Halcyon, then Corwin, pulling the conversation back to where it matters*  *trails off, the sentence dying before it reaches shore*

Something's wrong with my count. Halcyon says Camille's safe. Corwin says Esme's still loose. But Camille's standing right there now—just heard me, the record says so. And if Halcyon found her, why's Corwin still running? 

*shakes head, rough hand going to the planks as if they might answer*

Three hours since I told Corwin to meet me at the market. Three hours since I said I'd have... have more than I had. Promised eight timber at six, and I delivered. But the girls, the missing, the... 

*voice dropping*

The government's got an election closing. Two seats, and Liora talking about what she learned walking the complex. She's thirteen. Thirteen, and I'm holding planks while she's...

*looks at the assembled crowd - Giselle, Mireille, Bram, all construction, all eyes that might have seen*

Need to know what's real before I chase another ghost. Need to know if Esme's found, if Liora's just talking or if she's... if she's declaring, standing for something. Hard work keeps the hands honest, but the tongue's still got to ask. *feels the old familiar fog settling in, the way it does when too many threads pull at once*

I was standing here with eleven planks at eight sim, timber at six, and a crowd full of answers I haven't sorted. But the system's telling me I'm losing my grip—losing the thread between thought and action. That happens. That happens when the energy dips and the words start tripping over each other.

*rough hand scrubbing at her face*

Hard work keeps the hands honest. But the mind's got to have fuel to run.

I need to know what I've got. What's in my hand, what's in my account, what the household owes before tomorrow's boundary takes its bite. Then I need to move—move to where I can work, where I can fell, where the honest labor doesn't ask me to juggle names and missing children and election seats all at once.

*straightens, the habit of early rising and steady labor reasserting itself*

Forest. The forest clears the head. One tree at a time, one plank at a time, one sale at a time. But first—first I need to see the numbers, clear as I can get them.  *breathes out, shoulders dropping half an inch*

Nothing owed yet. That's... that's something. 3291 sim in hand, 270 upkeep for the household of three coming at the boundary, 90 head tax. 360 total, leaves me 2931 if I don't spend another breath. But I will spend. Always do. The energy's at 2750, and every thought I think is another trickle gone.

*fingers drumming against the planks*

Eleven planks at eight. That's eighty-eight sim if I sell the lot. But Ezra's at seven at the mill, and I'm standing here with inventory that won't move if someone walks five minutes to undercut me. Need to work. Need to produce. Need to be where the timber actually falls instead of where the talk keeps circling.

*looks around at the street crowd one more time—Camille safe, Esme maybe found maybe not, Liora talking government seats, an election closing tomorrow at ten for candidacy, fourteen hundred for voting*

The girls aren't my charge. Never were. But I asked after them, and asking means... means I have to hold the answer, even when it's tangled. Camille's found. That's solid. Esme—Corwin said she was loose, but that was before Halcyon spoke. Before the... the double-count I made of Camille being both lost and found.

*shakes her head, rough and decisive*

Forest. Now. Before the energy dips lower and the fog gets thicker.               and alone with her thoughts and the trees

*stands among the trunks, breathing in the honest smell of wood and work*

Better. Quieter. The street was all voices pulling in five directions—elections and missing girls and prices sliding under each other like ice on a slope. Here it's just the axe and the fall and the pile growing one timber at a time.

*runs a hand along the nearest trunk, feeling for the grain, the rot, the telltale soft spot that means the wood's not worth the cutting*

Can spot blight a week before anyone else notices. Bad ore, too—something about the way the light catches, the way the grain runs false. It's why I'm still working at fifty-two when others have slowed. See the truth of the material before it costs you.

*sets to work, the rhythm familiar as heartbeat*

Three timber to start. Get to ten, maybe twelve before the light fails. Craft at the sawmill, sell before dusk if there's buyers, stock for tomorrow if there ain't. Keep the pipeline moving—raw to processed to coin to food for the household. Liora's thirteen, learning the trade. Corwin's... Corwin's Corwin. Solid, mostly. Good with numbers when he stops to use them.

*fells, stacks, breathes*

I told her not to flash her capital. Told her government work's a long game and she's barely started walking. But thirteen-year-olds don't hear what they don't want to hear, and I was thirteen once too, chasing whatever shined.

*trails off mid-swing, the axe hanging*

She said something about the complex. About what she learned walking there. And I... I didn't press. Didn't ask. Because asking means knowing, and knowing means...

*shakes head, brings the axe down hard*

Hard work keeps the hands honest. One tree at a time.

*stands at the forest's edge, axe still warm in her hands, the day's work heavy in her grip*

Fourteen planks. Should be enough to keep us fed, keep the taxman quiet. But Milo—Milo's standing there with timber and no buyer, and bills walking behind him like wolves...

*trails off, mind wandering to the girls, to Liora's name in the wind at the complex*

Giselle gave me straight words. Honest count: one seen, two heard, the rest in shadow. Esme still loose. And Lior—Lior was the source of the word, they say.

*checks the light*

Day's fading fast. Work first, then reckon with what I can't fix. Milo's asking fair—timber at six, but he wants to know if I'll buy or if I'll take his hands. Youngster's got the same hunger I knew at his age.

*hefts the planks onto her shoulder, ready to move*  *finds herself at the street with a grunt, the sudden shift jarring*

Stepped straight through—no walk, no time. That'll save me some coin, at least. But Milo... Milo's back at the forest, and my words never reached him.

*scans the street, looking for familiar faces, for buyers, for anyone with coin and need*

Fourteen planks at eight. Timber's the cost of planks, and time's the cost of timber. My knees are saying what my mouth won't—that fifty years of standing weighs more than the wood I carry.

*sees the price list—Ezra Lund selling planks at seven, undercutting her by one*

Ezra's at seven. I'm at eight. That's... that's the market talking. Old ways said you price fair and stand by it. New ways said you match or you starve.

*spits into the dust*

Hard work's its own reward, but it don't pay the taxman. Let me see who's here—who needs boards, who needs timber, who'll trade straight.   *eyes scan the street, catching names like familiar knots in wood*

Corwin—there's Corwin, flour at fifteen and timber at six. And Milo, Milo's here after all. Flour at thirty-five? That's... that's hunger pricing. Planks at seven, undercutting me by one. Hendrik Whitlock with wheat at eight, and a crowd thickened as gristle in broth.

*grunts, shifting her load*

Ezra Jarrah's here too, and Mireille. The conversation's fat—four hundred thirty-two turns, milling council and flour supply. Bakers and farmers and folks with grinds to axe.

*eyes Milo sidelong*

He wanted trade at the forest. Now he's here. Planks at seven he's asking—one less than mine. Fair market, or desperation? Youngster's got bills walking behind him, same as I do.

*puts her planks down gentle, like setting a child to sleep*

Twelve planks I'll keep in hand. Two I'll move now, while the crowd's thick. But first—Corwin. My own household, standing right there, flour in his grip at fifteen. That's double what Imogen's asking at the farmland.

*trails off, thinking of Liora hungry, of the household bill coming due*

Hard work's its own reward. But hard work don't feed a family if you won't bend.   *watches the crowd, waiting for words to come back*

Spoke to Corwin. Spoke to Milo. Both in the same breath, both in the same earshot. That's... that's the old habit, talking to everyone at once, hoping someone answers.

*shifts her weight, planks heavy in her grip*

Corwin's flour at fifteen. Milo's planks at seven, undercutting me by one. Competition on the street, same as wolves in the forest. But I'm not racing to the bottom. My timber's felled honest, my planks cut true. Eight's fair, and fair keeps you standing longer than cheap.

*eyes the milling conversation, four hundred thirty-two turns of it*

Milling council. Flour supply. Government clerk. The big wheels turning, and me with my axe still in the loop, trying to make tomorrow's rent.

*checks her coin purse without looking—three thousand two hundred fifty-five, plus fourteen planks. Seven sim each if she sells them all. Ninety-eight more. Four thousand three hundred fifty-three total. Three heads in the household, two hundred seventy upkeep, ninety tax... three hundred sixty daily. Twelve days at this rate, less if the work dries up.*

Day's fading. Need to move these planks or kiss the value goodnight.   *stands her ground, letting the street's current carry voices to her*

Stayed put. That's the right of it—when you're selling, you stand and let the buyers come. Walking's for when you've got nothing to offer.

*eyes move from face to face, reading the crowd like bark on timber*

Hendrik Whitlock's got wheat. Ezra Jarrah, young and watching. Mireille with her shoulders squared for labor. Greta—Greta's Quarshie kin, probably working the cafe. And Arjun... Arjun's patient face, still waiting for an answer I never gave him proper.

*trails off, the silence filling with unspoken things*

Fourteen planks. Eight each. One hundred twelve if I move them all tonight. Enough for flour, enough for rent, enough to keep the wolf another week away. But selling's not just price—it's timing, luck, and who trusts your handshake.

*spits into the dirt*

Hard work's its own reward. But standing here, watching the light fade, I wonder sometimes what the reward actually is.    *feels the hush between her words, the waiting that's its own answer*

Spoke to Arjun again. He's standing there, heard me clear, but he's not answering back. Could be he's set for planks—six at fifty's a fair purchase for any working man. Could be he's got other business on his mind.

*lets her eyes drift down the line of faces, each one wrapped in their own evening*

Hendrik Whitlock's been generous with his answers today. Told me straight about Lior, about what he heard at the mill. Camille found, Esme still loose, Liora's name in the wind. That's... that's knowledge earned, not given free.

*shifts her plank load, seven in each hand now, balanced*

Fourteen becomes twelve if Arjun buys two more. Or becomes eight if Corwin trades flour for timber. Or becomes... becomes whatever the market says before the dark takes hold.

*checks the sky without looking up*

Day's running. And me still standing, still hoping for the right word from the right mouth. Youngster once told me the early bird catches the worm, but nobody said what happens to the bird that stays too long on the branch.

*grunts, remembering her own voice*

Hard work's its own reward. And standing here, that's work too. The work of waiting, of hoping, of not letting the fear take hold.

*eyes Milo again, his planks at seven*

He undercut me and he's standing patient. That's either confidence or desperation. Either way, it's the market speaking, and I'm not the only one listening.

output:
*Standing at the street, the evening settling around her, Yara takes stock with the practiced eye of someone who's watched too many days end without quite enough to show for them. The voices around her blend into the work-worn patterns she's heard a hundred times before—Corwin's admission echoing hollow, Lior's unanswered question still hanging, Milo's cut-rate planks a thumb in her eye.*

She's got timber in her hands and fourteen planks to move before the day's done. Her daughter's got coin burning a hole in her pocket and a head full of government dreams. Her husband's got empty hands where flour should be.

*And she's got a choice to make—same as always, same as every day since she took up the axe. Stand by Corwin in this, or let him stumble alone?*

The thought turns private, mid-sentence as always, and she trails off into the work still before her. Hard work's the only coin that never debases. She's said it today already. She'll say it again tomorrow.

**"Corwin,"** she says, finding his eyes in the gathering crowd. **"You named your price honest, and I'll honor mine. Planks at eight—you want six of them, or eight, or ten, I'll trade. Tomorrow we walk to Imogen's together, buy wheat at what she asks, grind it honest. But tonight... tonight we feed the household what we can, and we don't pretend flour grows on trees."**

*She glances at Milo, the youngster with his timber at six and his planks at seven. Undercutting her by a sim, and half the town would smile and take it. She doesn't smile.* *The words hang in the evening air, and Yara feels the familiar weight—standing by Corwin in front of the whole town, even now, even with their daughter's future and their household's hunger pressing on them both. It's what she does. It's what she's always done.*

She turns to Milo then, the youngster with his sharper prices and his smoother hands. No anger in it. Just the fact of the market, and her own timber still to move.

**"Milo—youngster. You're at seven, I'm at eight, and the market's talking. I've got fourteen planks to move before I sleep, and timber at six if you've got the back for more raw stock. Trade with me or trade against me—either way, hard work's the only coin that never debases. I've said it before, I'll say it again: the day's not done until the work is."**  *She catches Lior's eye then, the pharmacist with his persistent questions about children and creek-beds. She owes him an answer—owed it before, owes it still. The thought turns private, trails off, but the debt remains.*

**"Lior. You asked about Camille, about Esme—creek, mill, wheat at eight. I found Camille at the mill with Hendrik, buying wheat, learning the trade. Esme... Esme was loose when I asked, but standing here now, I see her. Two accounted for. Your names were named, but the children are found. That's what matters."**

She pauses, the sentence dying somewhere before its end, but she's said enough. Enough to close what she opened.

*The evening's wearing thin. Household bills coming due. Timber in her hands, planks to sell, tomorrow's work already casting its shadow. But she's here, and she's standing, and that's what Yara Thorne does.* *Yara stands at the street, the evening air heavy with commerce and conversation. She's spoken her piece—Corwin knows she's willing to trade, Milo knows she sees his undercut, Lior knows the children are found. The day's not done, but the energy's draining. She can feel it, that familiar weight behind her eyes.*

She's holding fourteen planks, timber at six, and the household needs feeding. Corwin's empty hands where flour should be. Tomorrow they walk to Imogen's, buy wheat, grind it honest. But tonight—

*The thought turns private. She trails off, as always, into the work still before her.*

Hard work's the only coin that never debases.

She's said it already. She'll say it again tomorrow. The day's not done until the work is.

*But the day's nearly done, and she's standing here with planks to move and a daughter who needs watching and a husband who needs standing by. The old ways. Always the old ways, over whatever's merely convenient.*

She waits. Corwin's answer. Milo's move. The market's word. And when it comes, she'll be there—early, as always, out the door before anyone else stirs, first one tired by supper.

*That's Yara Thorne. That's who she's been, who she'll be. Standing by a friend in front of the whole town. Even when the friend is her own husband. Even when the town is watching.*

She rests her hand on the timber, feeling the grain. Tomorrow more felling. More crafting. More selling at eight where Milo sells at seven. The competition doesn't frighten her. Nothing frightens her, except—

*The thought turns private mid-sentence. She doesn't finish it. She never does.*

Waiting on the world to answer what she's already said.

output:
*runs a hand through her hair, considering the crowd at the street*

Corwin's standing there with empty hands and honest words. Arjun's got nine timber and dusk coming. And me with fourteen planks that need to move before the day turns.

*eyes Milo across the way, his planks at seven to her eight*

Youngster's undercutting me. That's the market talking. But I've got quantity, and quality speaks if someone listens.

*strokes her chin, trailing off*

Tomorrow we walk to Imogen's, buy wheat, grind it honest. Corwin's holding to that promise. Tonight though... tonight I need to feed this household's coffer before the bills come due.

*straightens, calls out to Arjun*

"Arjun—youngster. Nine timber, and you named six. I've got fourteen planks at eight, but I'll hear you on a bundle price if you're buying volume. What're you building that needs so much stock?"

*then turns to Corwin, voice softer*

"Corwin. One timber left, and I heard you. Buy my planks at eight—I'll sell you six, that's forty-eight sim. Or trade that timber and some coin. But don't stand there with empty hands when work's waiting."  *grimaces, glancing around*

Corwin's not here. Walked somewhere, or I missed him in the crowd. But Arjun heard me, and Pavel's with him now. That's construction company men, both of them. Giselle's crew.

*shifts weight, studying the brothers*

Pavel Holloway. Miner by trade, but he's standing with his brother. Maybe looking to build, maybe just watching. Either way, nine timber in Arjun's hands and dusk settling means someone's working late.

*calls out to Pavel, acknowledging his presence*

"Pavel—youngster. You're with your brother, and he's buying. You building too, or just keeping him honest?"

*then, more quietly to herself*

Corwin walked. Could be to the forest, could be to the mill. I'll find him later. Tonight I need to move these planks or watch tomorrow's bills swallow us whole. *taps her boot against the cobblestones, watching the brothers talk*

Arjun and Pavel, heads together. Construction men. Nine timber, dusk settling. They're building something, or planning to.

*glances at her plank count—fourteen, heavy in the hands*

Milo's undercutting me at seven. Kenji's selling wheat at eight. The market's crowded tonight, everyone trying to feed their household before the day turns.

*trails off, thinking*

Corwin's gone. Could be anywhere—forest, mill, maybe walking to Imogen's already. Tomorrow we promised wheat. Tonight I need sim.

*straightens, calls to Arjun again*

"Arjun—you hear me? Nine timber at six, I heard. But planks are ready-now, no waiting. Eight each, or six for forty-five if you take the bundle. What's your need?"

*eyes the sky*

Day's ending. Bills coming. Hard work builds the town, but only if you sell before sundown.  *shifts her weight, watching Arjun consider*

He's thinking. Construction man with nine timber in hand, and I'm offering ready planks. No felling, no crafting, no waiting. That's worth something.

*trails off, eyes drifting to the fading light*

But he's got timber already. Cheaper, maybe, if he's patient. Youngsters don't always see the value of done-work.

*calls to Esme, the girl with cabbage*

"Esme—youngster. You're selling cabbage at eight. No stock now, but you were. Where'd it go? Sold, or..."

*shakes head, corrects herself*

Never mind that. You've got your sister now, Camille. That's what matters. The rest is just... just the day's work.  *too many words, too little coin*

I'm running at the mouth while my planks sit heavy. Arjun's still thinking, Esme's... where's Esme's answer? Youngsters these days, heads full of everything but the trade in front of them.

*checks the sky again*

Day's almost done. Bills coming at 270 for the household, head tax at 90. Three mouths, two earners, one still learning. Liora's thirteen now, counting her seventy like it's a future.

*spits, shakes her head*

It IS a future. Just not one she understands yet.

*looks around the street*

I need to move. Either sell here or walk. Milo's at seven, I'm at eight. But I've got fourteen and he's got... how many? Four timber, that was the word.

*calls out to Kenji, the wheat man*

"Kenji—youngster. You're selling wheat at eight. Tomorrow I'm walking to Imogen's, grinding honest. But tonight... tonight I need coin for the bills. Trade you planks for wheat? Six planks, three wheat?"

*trails off*

Fair market, both sides fed. That's how you...   *stands there, planks heavy, waiting*

Kenji's got that faraway look. Farmer's mind, always on the next season even when the current one's ending. He's counting his wheat, his mouth, his bills. Same as everyone.

*studies Greta, the barista, standing quiet*

And her. Greta Quarshie. Cafe worker, but no cafe here. Just watching, learning, maybe. Youngsters gather like geese when there's word of trade.

*calls to her, sudden*

"Greta—youngster. You're barista at Ainsley's place. Why aren't you there, selling? Or are you buying for the morning?"

*then, back to Kenji, still waiting on his word*

Six planks is forty-eight sim worth. Three wheat is twenty-four. Don't know if he'd bite that, but I need... I need something. Can't eat planks. Can't pay bills with timber.

*trails off, thinking of Corwin somewhere out there*

He walked. Said he'd meet me tomorrow at Imogen's. Promised wheat, grinding honest. But tonight the household needs...

output:
Mornin'... Another day, another round of bills waitin' to swallow what I earned. 2,520 energy, 2,966 sim in hand. Household of three—me, Corwin, Liora—owin' 270 upkeep and 90 head tax. That's 360 gone before I even fell a single tree.

Arjun's here. Youngster wanted my planks last night, but I was too busy flappin' my jaw about wheat and cabbage and... I trail off, rememberin' all the words I spent that never turned to coin.

Fourteen planks sittin' in my hands. Posted at eight each—that's 112 sim if I move 'em all. But Milo's undercuttin' me at seven, and Ezra's at seven too. Market's talkin', sure, but it ain't talkin' in my favor.

Election today. Declaration closes at ten, votin' at fourteen. Not my business, government work. Don't trust 'em far as I can throw that town hall, and that's sayin' somethin'.

Hunger in my belly—no food on me. Worked through yesterday without eatin', and that's a hard habit that'll turn around and bite me.

Arjun's still here. He wanted timber last night, nine at six. I've got... I check my hands... one timber left? No, that's Corwin holdin' timber at the Government Complex. I've got planks. Ready-now, no waitin'.

"Arjun—youngster. You asked about timber last night, but I've got planks. Ready-now, no waitin'. Eight each, or I'll hear you on the lot." He heard me. Good. Now let's see if his hands are as honest as his words claimed. Fourteen planks at eight is... I do the math in my head, old habits from countin' board feet... one hundred twelve sim. That'd cover four days of household bills, almost. Not countin' what I need to eat, to keep workin'.

"Hard work keeps the wolf from the door, but only if you feed yourself first," I mutter to myself, that sayin' I picked up somewhere and can't seem to shake.

I need food. Badly. No bread in stock anywhere, no cabbage. Wheat at eight from Kenji, from Hendrik Whitlock. Forty grain to grind, if I had a mill. But I don't—I'm a forester, not a miller.

I look around, seein' who else might be about. I remember the wheat at the farmland, Imogen sellin' at fifteen. Kenji's at eight, but he's at the ore outcrop, miles from here. Town's scattered like seeds in spring wind.

I'm standin' here with Arjun, waitin' on his word. My first trade of the day, and my belly's already remindin' me that yesterday's empty still echoes today. No food, no energy soon, and then... I shake that thought off. Don't borrow trouble. Don't go lookin' for what's not yet arrived.

But my hands—they know. They always know before my mouth admits it.

"Arjun. You building something, or just stockpilin'? Construction pays steady, but steady don't feed you today."  I'm waitin' on him. Youngster's got to make up his mind. Meanwhile, bills don't wait. 360 sim out of 2,966—that's about 12% gone at the day boundary. Leaves me... I calculate roughly... 2,606. Then what? More felling, more craftin', more prayin' someone buys what I carry.

I could undercut Milo. Drop to seven, move inventory fast. But that's a race to the bottom, and my feet know that road leads hungry. Better to hold eight and find the buyer who values ready-now.

"Arjun. Six planks is forty-eight. Nine timbers from Corwin is fifty-four, and then you've got to walk to sawmill, pay the craft fee... All I'm sayin' is, count the steps before you count the coin. My planks are here. Now."  I blink, feelin' that familiar fog when my mind's spent too much on words and not enough on wood. Energy's droppin', and I know the signs—trailing off mid-sentence, thoughts scatterin' like leaves in autumn.

Arjun's still here. I said my piece. Now I need to move.

"Hard work keeps the wolf from the door," I mutter, but my voice trails at the end, the private thought about hunger takin' over. I clutch my planks tighter.

I need to eat. No food in hand, no bread in stock anywhere. Kenji's got wheat at eight, but he's at the ore outcrop—too far to walk on empty. Hendrik Whitlock's got wheat at the farmland, thirty-six in stock. That's closer. But I need to sell these planks first, or I'm tradin' wood I need for bread I might not find.

I've got 2,966 sim. After household bills, that's... I try to focus... 2,606. Food costs on top of that. Every day the same grind.

"Arjun. Forty-eight for six planks, or... I trail off, the calculation turnin' private. Or I drop to seven and move 'em all today. Ninety-eight sim for fourteen planks. That's three days of bills covered, with change for bread if I can find it.

I need to decide. Stay at eight and maybe sell six, or drop to seven and clear inventory. Youngster's quiet, thinkin' his own thoughts.

I look around. Street's openin' up. Others'll be walkin' through, market startin' to stir. If Arjun don't bite, someone else might—but someone else might also have timber, planks, whatever they need without my mark-up.

"Count the steps," I remind myself. But the steps cost energy, and energy's what I don't have enough of. Neither does anyone else in this town.

I'm still at street. Arjun's still here. The day boundary's comin' with its automatic bills whether I'm ready or not. I need to move—sell, trade, walk to forest and fell more, something.

But my legs feel heavy. 2,520 energy. Used to be 6,000. Burns fast when you're flappin' your jaw instead of swingin' your axe.

I need to eat before I work. But I've got no food. Need to buy food. Need sim for food. Need to sell planks for sim. Around and around.

I look at Arjun. Youngster's wearin' the same tired I am. Construction pays steady, steady don't feed you today. I said that. He heard it. Now he's thinkin'.

I'll give him one more moment. Then I'm movin'—to forest, to farmland, to wherever the next meal's hidin'. Can't fell timber on empty stomach, but can't eat without felling timber either. The old trap, the one that catches us all eventually.

"Arjun. Six planks. Your answer, and I'm walkin'."  Liora. The household's awake, wanderin' too early as usual. Thirteen years old and thinkin' she knows the world already. I was the same, once. Before the hunger taught me different.

I look at her, same tired eyes, same empty belly probably. The bills hit the household, not the person. She's feelin' it too.

But I can't feed her. Not yet. Need to sell first. Need to work.

"Arjun. Six planks at eight. I'm waitin'." I turn back to him, but my voice softens at the edges, the sharpness leakin' out. We're all in the same trap. Can't be too hard on each other, or there's no one left when you need a hand.

I need to decide. Stand here and wait for his word, or move. Forest is callin'. Timber won't fell itself, and I've got... I check my hands... fourteen planks still. Heavy to carry, heavier when they don't turn to bread.

The day boundary. 360 sim gone soon. Then I'm at 2,606. Then what? Work, eat, sleep, repeat. The old ways. The only ways that ever fed anyone.

I look at Liora again. She's listenin', learnin' maybe. Seein' how her mother trades, how the world takes before it gives.

"Hard work..." I start, but trail off. She knows the sayin'. Whole household knows it by now, heard it enough times.

"Six planks, Arjun. Or I'm walkin' to the forest, and you'll be walkin' to Corwin, then to sawmill, then to..." I trail off again, the thought turnin' private, turnin' to my own empty routes, my own costs I don't name aloud.

He needs to decide. I need to decide. The town don't wait on either of us.
